Neonatal Dwarf lanternsharks emerge from their egg cases at a remarkably small size, with field surveys off the coasts of Colombia and Venezuela indicating a total length at birth of 5.75 centimeters [Lb = 5.75 centimeters]. This diminutive starting dimension reflects the species' status within the family Etmopteridae as one of the smallest known elasmobranchs and imposes a narrow window for initial prey capture in the deep, dimly lit continental slopes they inhabit. The yolk-sac resorption process is rapid in these shallow inshore nursery zones, and pups begin independent foraging on small crustaceans within days of parturition. Given their minute body size and the energetic demands of early growth, mortality during the first few months is presumed to be high, though precise survivorship estimates remain unavailable for wild populations. The small birth length also constrains the range of ingestible prey items, restricting neonates to copepods and other microcrustaceans until their jaw apparatus matures sufficiently to handle larger, more muscular prey.

As individuals approach the upper boundary of somatic growth, adults attain a maximum recorded total length of 21.5 centimeters [Li = 21.5 centimeters], a value that places Etmopterus perryi among the tiniest chondrichthyans globally, within the order Squaliformes. This ultimate total length is associated with a corresponding ultimate wet weight of approximately 30.0 grams [Wwi = approximately 30.0 grams], a value derived from scaling relationships observed in the spiny dogfish Squalus acanthias. The attainment of this asymptotic size generally occurs by the time individuals are several years old, although chronological age data for this species remain scarce. At such a modest body mass, the metabolic costs of daily activity are low, and the species likely sustains itself on a diet of small squid and mesopelagic shrimp. The compact body plan of the Dwarf lanternshark also facilitates its characteristic bioluminescent displays, which are used for counter-illumination and possibly intraspecific signaling in the dim bathyal environment.

Sexual maturation proceeds differently between the sexes, with females reaching puberty at a total length of 15.75 centimeters [Lp = 15.75 centimeters], while males become reproductively active at a slightly larger size of 17.75 centimeters [Lp = 17.75 centimeters]. This divergence in the total length at puberty suggests that females allocate resources to gonadal development earlier than males, a pattern commonly observed in elasmobranchs where females must accommodate developing embryos within a limited coelomic cavity. The onset of gonadal maturation is accompanied by thickening of the oviducal gland epithelia in females and elongation of the claspers in males. Field dissections have revealed that gravid individuals typically carry small litters, and the synchrony between ovarian maturation and sperm storage from previous copulations allows for continuous reproductive readiness. The physiological trigger for this maturation appears to be more closely tied to body size than to chronological age, an adaptation to the unpredictable food availability of the deep sea.

Reproductive output in this species has been quantified under controlled conditions, where at a stable water temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], the maximum reproduction rate is approximately 2.5 pups per year [Ri = approximately 2.5 pups per year]. This figure is characteristic of a k-selected life-history strategy within the Etmopteridae, in which low fecundity is offset by relatively high maternal investment per offspring. Gestation is presumed to be lengthy, and the small brood sizes likely minimize the metabolic burden on the mother during the energetically demanding period of embryonic development. The cool thermal regime of the deep bathyal zone (typically 7 to 10 °C) further slows metabolic processes, reinforcing the low intrinsic rate of increase that distinguishes this species from more fecund, shallower-water elasmobranchs within the Squaliformes.

The life-history profile of the Dwarf lanternshark, characterized by its minute birth length of only 5.75 centimeters [Lb = 5.75 centimeters] and modest adult body mass reaching approximately 30.0 grams [Wwi = approximately 30.0 grams], underscores the extreme miniaturization that has occurred within the subfamily Etmopterinae. In a comparative context, the ultimate total length of just 21.5 centimeters [Li = 21.5 centimeters] places this species at the lower extreme of the size distribution for all described Squaliformes, and its reproductive rate of roughly 2.5 pups per year [Ri = roughly 2.5 pups per year] at 9 °C [T = 9 °C] is correspondingly among the lowest recorded for any chondrichthyan. The pubertal size of 15.75 centimeters [Lp = 15.75 centimeters] for females and 17.75 centimeters [Lp = 17.75 centimeters] for males represents a life-history bottleneck where somatic growth must be balanced against the onset of gonadal maturation. These intertwined constraints—small body size, low fecundity, and slow maturation—render Etmopterus perryi particularly vulnerable to any increase in natural or anthropogenic mortality, and the species' long generation time makes population recovery exceedingly slow following disturbance.
